props.title: One Missed Call

sections.content: One Missed Call (2003), directed by Takashi Miike, emerged during J-horror's golden age alongside Ringu (1998) and Ju-On: The Grudge (2002). Miike transforms the ubiquitous cell phone into a harbinger of death, where victims receive voicemails dated in the future containing their own final moments. The film's genius lies in corrupting the intimacy of personal technology - much like Pulse (2001) did with the internet. Miike's signature extreme style is surprisingly restrained here, building dread through the inexorable march toward each predicted death rather than graphic violence. One Missed Call|2003|College students receive voicemails from their future selves moments before death|Shudder Ringu|1998|A cursed videotape kills viewers seven days after watching|Prime Video Pulse|2001|Ghosts invade the world through internet connections|Criterion Channel

The film's technological anxiety tapped into millennial fears about our growing dependence on mobile devices. While Phone (2002) and Cellular (2004) used similar premises for straightforward thrillers, Miike infuses One Missed Call with distinctly Japanese elements - particularly the "dead wet girl" motif popularized by Dark Water (2002). The haunted ringtone became as iconic as the video static in Ringu or the death rattle in Ju-On. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

Despite spawning two Japanese sequels and an inferior American remake in 2008, the original One Missed Call stands as a pivotal entry in the techno-horror subgenre. Its influence can be seen in later films like Unfriended (2014) and Countdown (2019), which similarly weaponize everyday technology. The film's blend of supernatural revenge and technological terror created a template for modern digital horror like Host (2020).
